# Q5: In a paragraph, summarise your findings and suggest directions for future research.

Across the four study arms, our findings highlight the complex relationship between genetic susceptibility, molecular changes and treatment responses in Parkinson's disease (PD). Population genetics analysis revealed significantly higher polygenic risk scores (PRS) in PD patients compared with healthy controls, although substantial overlap between groups limited their predictive value. RNA-seq analysis identified 30 differentially expressed genes, with upregulated genes associated with dopamine biosynthesis and downregulated genes associated with oxidative stress responses, suggesting that disruptions to these pathways may contribute to PD pathology. Drug screening identified four compounds associated with significantly increased neuronal viability following MPP exposure, three of which targeted genes (MOXD1, SULT1A1 and MAOA) that were also upregulated in PD, highlighting potential therapeutic targets involved in dopamine regulation. Clinical trial analysis found that the new compound and exercise were associated with improved balance, while increasing age was associated with decreased balance. Although PRS was not significantly associated with balance overall, a treatment-specific association suggested that genetic risk may influence treatment response. However, these findings are limited by small sample sizes, reliance on technical replicates in the drug screen and incomplete donor information, which prevented linking all four datasets at the participant level. Future research should investigate additional genetic and environmental risk factors in larger, independent cohorts, validate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of the identified compounds, and explore whether genetic and transcriptional profiles can predict clinical treatment responses. Integrating these approaches may improve our understanding of PD pathology and support the development of more targeted therapeutic strategies.
